steps: Draw the base AB of length 4 cm.
With the compass set to 4 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
Keep the compass at 4 cm, put the point on B, and draw a second arc that crosses the first.
Mark the crossing point C. It is on the arc from A, so AC = 4 cm, and on the arc from B, so BC = 4 cm.
Join AC and BC. All three sides are 4 cm.
Draw the base AB = 4 cm.
With the compass set to 5 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
Set the compass to 6 cm, put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the first arc.
The crossing point is C. It is 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B. Join AC and BC.
Check with the ruler: AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm.
Take 8 cm as the base AB. Draw an arc of 3 cm from A and an arc of 4 cm from B.
From A, the arc reaches 3 cm along the base and the arc from B reaches 4 cm back, which covers 3 + 4 = 7 cm of the 8 cm. They do not meet.
For 2, 3 and 6, take 6 cm as the base. The arcs of 2 cm and 3 cm cover 2 + 3 = 5 cm of the 6 cm and do not meet.
In both sets the two shorter lengths add to less than the longest: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6.

M1.S7.T7.C22#0.question: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle for each of the following sets of lengths? (a) 10 km, 10 km and 25 km; (b) 5 mm, 10 mm and 20 mm; (c) 12 cm, 20 cm and 40 cm

steps: Write the lengths in increasing order: p, q, r with p ≤ q ≤ r.
The length r is the longest, so p < q + r is true because q + r is already at least r, which is at least p. Also q < p + r, because p + r is at least r, which is at least q.
Only the comparison for r, r < p + q, can fail.
Test with 7, 10, 15: 7 < 10 + 15 = 25 and 10 < 7 + 15 = 22 hold, and the longest check 15 < 7 + 10 = 17 holds too. For 10, 15, 30 the first two hold and only the longest check, 30 < 25, fails.
So at least two comparisons always hold, and the two that always hold belong to the two shorter lengths. Only the longest length needs a check.

M2.S19.T19.C56#0.question: In triangle ABC, ∠B = 50° and ∠C = 70°. Using a line through A and parallel to BC, find ∠A.
steps: Draw the line XY through A, parallel to BC.
∠XAB and ∠B are alternate angles, so ∠XAB = 50°. ∠YAC and ∠C are alternate angles, so ∠YAC = 70°.
∠XAB, ∠BAC and ∠YAC together make the straight angle XAY: 50° + ∠BAC + 70° = 180°.
Construct to check: with 50° at B and 70° at C, the angle measured at A is 60°.

steps: Draw a line XY through A, parallel to BC.
Alternate angles give ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C.
∠XAB, ∠A and ∠YAC together make a straight angle: ∠XAB + ∠A + ∠YAC = 180°.
Replace ∠XAB by ∠B and ∠YAC by ∠C: ∠B + ∠A + ∠C = 180°.
Paper fold: fold the three corners of a paper triangle in so that they meet at one point on the base. The three angles sit side by side along the straight base, which is 180°.
Keep the ruler along the base BC, and place the set square on the ruler with one edge of its right angle against the ruler.
Slide the set square along the ruler until its upright edge touches A.
Draw along the upright edge down from A to BC. This segment AD is the altitude.
AD is perpendicular to BC, so the angle at D is 90°, and the length of AD is the height from BC to A.
Draw AC = 5 cm. The angle at B is 90°, so ∠A + ∠C = 90°.
Choose ∠A = 30°, then ∠C = 60°, and the arms cross at B. Choose ∠A = 45°, then ∠C = 45°. Choose ∠A = 70°, then ∠C = 20°. Each choice gives a different triangle.
Any value strictly between 0° and 90° can be chosen for ∠A, and ∠C is then 90° − ∠A.
There are infinitely many values to choose from, so there are infinitely many different triangles.
